Ovarian aging

PBM changed ovarian measures in aged-mouse studies. A small uncontrolled human pilot found a higher antral follicle count but no significant rise in oocyte yield. A separate blood-irradiation study found biomarker changes, not evidence of improved fertility.

Publications and records

3publications

Publication and study types

  • Human nonrandomized controlled study1
  • Human single-arm study1
  • Animal (mouse)2
  • In-vitro cell study1

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Antral follicle count — In a single-arm pilot of ten women with diminished ovarian reserve, median AFC increased from 2 (IQR 1–5) to 6 (IQR 2–7; p = 0.011) after 630-nm LED treatment (Su et al. 2026).

Oocytes retrieved — In the same pilot, the median changed from 2 (IQR 1–5) to 5 (IQR 2–7; p = 0.083), which was not statistically significant. The before-and-after comparison had no control group (Su et al. 2026).

AMH and antral follicle count — In a separate nonrandomized ILIB comparison of 75 women, the reported changes were not statistically significant (Lin et al. 2024).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low certainty for selected ovarian-function measures in aged-mouse models (He et al. 2024; Su et al. 2026).

Very low certainty for ovarian-reserve or fertility benefit in women. Human evidence consists of one nonrandomized study and one small single-arm pilot, with no significant improvement in AMH, AFC, or retrieved-oocyte count (Lin et al. 2024; Su et al. 2026).

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications address PBM in ovarian aging: one study examined aged mice and cultured human granulosa cells, one studied intravascular laser blood irradiation in women with age-related ovarian decline, and one tested a wearable red-light device in women with diminished ovarian reserve. These studies assess different interventions and outcomes and do not represent replicated human trials.

Human and clinical evidence

A nonrandomized controlled study of 75 infertile women used intravascular laser blood irradiation (ILIB). It reported altered cumulus-cell gene expression related to oxidative-stress response and energy metabolism. Changes in anti-Müllerian hormone and antral follicle count were not statistically significant, and the gene-expression findings are not evidence of improved fertility (Lin et al. 2024).

A single-arm pilot enrolled ten women with diminished ovarian reserve for daily 630-nm LED exposure before egg retrieval. Antral follicle count increased, but oocyte yield did not increase significantly. Without a control group, this before-and-after observation cannot establish a treatment effect (Su et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

In naturally aged mice, 650-nm PBM improved hormone, follicle, angiogenesis, apoptosis, oxidative-stress, and mitochondrial measures (He et al. 2024). A separate aged-mouse study compared red 630-nm with near-infrared 850-nm light. The 630-nm treatment improved pregnancy and litter outcomes, while 850-nm light did not improve those outcomes (Su et al. 2026).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

In hydrogen-peroxide-stressed KGN human granulosa cells, PBM increased viability, proliferation, hormone secretion, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP, while reducing apoptosis and oxidative-stress measures. These results concern a stressed cell line, not intact human ovaries (He et al. 2024).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The aged-mouse study used a 650-nm semiconductor laser at 80 mW and 6.7 mW/cm² for five or ten minutes, corresponding to 2 or 4 J/cm². The reported ovarian improvements were at 4 J/cm² (He et al. 2024). The later mouse experiment delivered 630-nm red or 850-nm near-infrared LED light at 50 mW/cm² for five minutes daily over 15 days, or 15 J/cm² per day (Su et al. 2026).

In women, the wearable device delivered 630-nm light at 15 mW/cm² for 30 minutes daily until the day before retrieval, or 27 J/cm² per day. The ILIB study used intravascular 633-nm red light over 20 sessions (Su et al. 2026; Lin et al. 2024). These routes and doses are not interchangeable, and no study established an optimal human regimen.

Interpretation

Animal studies show model-specific changes, including a wavelength-specific pregnancy and litter result. Human studies are exploratory: one lacked random allocation and found no significant AMH or AFC changes, while the other lacked a control group and had no significant increase in retrieved oocytes. The evidence does not show that PBM improves pregnancy or live-birth rates in women.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two aged-mouse experiments found changes in ovarian function, but only the study using 630-nm red light reported better pregnancy and litter outcomes. Human reports are nonrandomized or single-arm. The larger ILIB comparison found no significant AMH or AFC change, and the ten-woman pilot had no significant oocyte-yield increase. Neither establishes a fertility benefit in women (He et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2024; Su et al. 2026).
